title: How knowledge is structured for experts: If-then statements
author: Ollie Lovell
summary: Ollie Lovell argues that when students describe their learning only in terms of surface topic labels -- "we're doing titrations," "we're doing Pythagoras' theorem" -- they are missing the why and when of what they've learned, and proposes that teachers instead help students structure their knowledge as "if-then" statements. The basic form ("if I want to achieve outcome Y, then I can take action X") mirrors, he argues, how expert knowledge is actually organised across disciplines, from graphic design to architecture to music. Lovell shows how if-then statements can be nested to represent increasing depth of expertise, illustrating with a musician's progression from a simple major/minor key association to the specific pivot chords an expert would know for transitioning between keys. He then reworks his opening classroom examples into if-then form, showing how a chemistry, biology, maths, or art student could describe not just what they are doing but the condition-action logic behind it. Lovell closes by suggesting teachers explicitly map out the if-then statements they want built into long-term memory during lesson planning, framing this as the core of the teacher's role: helping novices acquire the knowledge structures experts already possess.
points: Lovell's if-then framework reframes classroom knowledge as condition-action pairs ("if you want outcome Y, then you can take action X"), which he argues is how expert knowledge is actually structured across disciplines.
If-then statements can be nested to represent progressively deeper expertise, illustrated through a musician's progression from a basic major/minor association to specific pivot-chord knowledge.

Lovell contrasts topic-label answers ("we're doing Pythagoras' theorem") with if-then answers ("if you have a right-angled triangle and two side lengths, then you can use Pythagoras' Theorem") to show what students are missing when they can only name a topic.
He recommends teachers explicitly map the if-then statements they want students to retain during lesson planning, rather than leaving that condition-action logic implicit.
quotes: As teachers, our primary role is to help novice learners to acquire the knowledge of experts.
An oft-overlooked knowledge structure that encapsulates much of the knowledge of experts if the humble if-then statement.
If a graphic designer wants to emphasize text in a layout but avoid using bold or italics, then they can increase the letter spacing for added emphasis.
All of this knowledge is stored as if-then statements. And these statements are ‘nested’, representing deeper and deeper, more and more detailed knowledge.
It helps us to recognise that those students who answered that they were 'doing titrations' or 'doing Pythagoras' theorem' were lacking key information.
During the lesson planning process, it’s beneficial for teachers to consider the if-then statements they want students to build into long-term memory.
